scenario: AITA for 'stealing' my Dad's business idea and making a success of it? | Title says it all really. I (26M) technically ''stole'' my dad's business idea. When I first heard it from him, it was so simple yet so...genius. I can't say exactly what it is here, but it was genius. The thing is, me and my dad (55M) are complete opposites. He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). Physically, I look more like my grandad, but personality wise, I guess I'm a bit more impulsive and hot headed and not as intelligent as my dad, but I get things done. Perhaps I'm more ''traditional masculine'' than my dad. Its like I should be in the older generation, and he should be from the newer one. When I heard my Dad's business idea, I was amazed, but I didn't truly believe my Dad could pull it off. He doesn't get things done. He's always been full of great ideas, but ideas not put to use are useless. So I took the idea and ran with it. I got IP rights and started the business with it 2 years ago. Since then, its been a massive success. Not millions or anything, but into the six figures and the potential to make millions is there perhaps in the next half decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. Well I confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels and he said I'm a ''fucking asshole''. He said he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. AITA?

I do my shalat five times a day and every Friday I go to the mosque for Jumuah — the same place, the same people, every week. A lot of how I think about right and wrong gets shaped by those conversations and that environment. Do you think being surrounded by the same religious community like that changes how people see things?

Being part of a consistent religious community, such as attending Friday prayers at the same mosque with the same people, significantly influences one's perspective and belief system. Here's a structured summary of the thought process and conclusions: 1. **Reinforcement of Beliefs**: The repetitive exposure to similar opinions and teachings within the community reinforces existing beliefs. This can lead to a stronger alignment with the community's values, often without critical questioning. 2. **Environmental Influence**: The mosque serves as a multifaceted environment for worship, learning, and community engagement. Teachings here shape a moral framework, emphasizing values like charity, which may prioritize certain ethical standards in daily life. 3. **Diversity of Opinions**: The homogeneity of opinions within the community might limit exposure to diverse perspectives, potentially hindering critical thinking. However, a supportive community can foster confidence in shared values. 4. **Role of Religious Leaders**: Leaders significantly influence the community's beliefs, emphasizing certain practices or doctrines. This can affect interactions with outsiders and the perception of essential vs. non-essential practices. 5. **Critical Thinking and Questioning**: A community that discourages dissent may limit the exploration of alternative viewpoints, leading to a more homogeneous belief system. Conversely, a community that encourages learning can foster a nuanced perspective. 6. **Long-term Effects**: Consistent exposure to the same environment can solidify beliefs, providing a stable moral compass. However, it may also limit adaptability to new information or changing circumstances. **Conclusion**: The religious community plays a crucial role in shaping one's perspective, reinforcing values, and providing a supportive environment. However, it is essential to balance this with exposure to diverse viewpoints to ensure a well-rounded and critically assessed belief system.

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I did the right thing or not. Let me start by understanding the situation. I took my dad's business idea, and now it's been a big success. But my dad is really upset about it. He feels betrayed, and even my sister is siding with him. On the other hand, my mom and granddad support me. I offered him 20% of the profits, but he refused and told me to get out. I think he's being unreasonable, but I'm not entirely sure. First, I need to think about the concept of stealing an idea. Is taking someone's idea without their consent considered stealing? In a business context, ideas are valuable, and people often protect them with patents or copyrights. But in this case, it was just an idea my dad had, and I took it and ran with it. Did I steal it, or did I just use it? I also need to consider the dynamics between me and my dad. He's more introverted and has always been intelligent but hasn't been able to execute his ideas. I, on the other hand, am more action-oriented and have been able to turn ideas into reality. So, in a way, I took his idea and gave it the execution it needed. But does that make it right? Another angle is the emotional impact on my dad. He felt betrayed, and that's a strong emotion. Betrayal can damage relationships, and in this case, it's affecting our family dynamics. My sister is upset with me, and my dad is hurt. Even though my mom and granddad support me, the fact that my dad is so upset is significant. I also need to think about the offer I made to give him 20% of the profits. That shows that I value his contribution and want to make things right. But he rejected it, which might indicate that he's more hurt by the principle of me taking his idea than the financial aspect. Maybe I should have talked to him first before taking the idea and starting the business. Communication is key in relationships, especially family ones. If I had discussed it with him, maybe he would have felt more involved and less betrayed. On the other hand, I might have thought that since he wasn't able to execute the idea, it was better for me to take it and make it successful. But that decision might have come at the cost of damaging our relationship. I also wonder about the long-term implications. If I continue to handle this situation the way I did, will it affect our family ties permanently? Or is there a way to reconcile and move forward? Perhaps I should consider seeking a mediator or talking to a family therapist to help navigate this conflict. It might be easier to address these issues with a neutral third party involved. In summary, while I might have made a successful business by taking my dad's idea, the emotional and relational costs seem high. It's important to balance ambition with respect for family relationships and to communicate openly to avoid misunderstandings and hurt feelings.
